X is second. It is a tidy single file and also encodes non-ASCII Location headers, so it never returns 500 on a redirect. Against it: HEAD requests count clicks, the per-IP limiter arrays are unbounded, there is no handler for listen errors, frontend tests are thinner, and the README is minimal.

Z is third. It is compact and well documented, and its tests are reasonable. But it has a real correctness bug: a valid absolute https URL containing non-Latin-1 characters, or one with CR/LF, is accepted with 201 and then returns 500 on redirect, after already counting a click. It also has an unbounded limiter, reads oversized bodies in full, and its tests write into public/ and depend on hard-coded POST counts.

reasoning: X and Z both meet the spec line by line under the black-box probe, including the edge cases: the exact body-size boundary, rejected POSTs counting toward the limit, parallel bursts held to exactly 20, an unset admin token, traversal attempts, and non-ASCII redirects. Both validate URLs strictly and compare the admin token safely. The gap between them is small. X wins on code structure: small single-purpose modules and a factory with injectable clock, limit and public dir. Its frontend is more polished: busy state, a friendly network-error message, safe link rendering, formatted dates and a copy button. It also has sharper boundary and ordering tests: exactly 10240 bytes, 429 before 415, unit tests for the limiter, and traversal against a secret-file fixture. Z wins on reliably delivering error responses: it drains bodies, so the 413 arrived for every upload size, while X's Connection: close often resets the client on large streamed uploads. Z also has persistence and DOM-rendering tests and adds CSP and graceful shutdown. X's close-on-413 is a defensible resource-protection choice and only affects oversized streaming uploads, so I rank X first by a narrow margin. Y is functionally correct on the core contract, but it is clearly weaker. Its new URL()-only check accepts whitespace, CR/LF, 'http:example.com' and leading spaces. Its rate limiter has no per-IP cap and no idle pruning, which is a memory and CPU growth vector. It also uses message-regex duplicate detection, modulo-biased code generation and a length-leaking token compare. Its tests are thinner and skip the rolling-window and persistence checks.
